instructions:
Voice Affect: calm, curious and clear.
Tone: conversational mathematical teaching for a bright sixteen-year-old.
Pacing: steady and unhurried; give numerical examples room to land.
Pronunciation: read formulas as the supplied words; modulus means the divisor in a remainder rule.
Delivery: no imitation of any person or branded presentation style.

clips.text: Can a finite list of repeating number patterns catch every integer? Start with twelve positions on a clock. Colour every even position. Then add multiples of three. Some positions remain empty. We can keep adding remainder rules until none do.

Next take numbers leaving remainder one on division by four, then remainder five on division by six, then remainder seven on division by twelve. Every clock position is covered. Because all five divisors divide twelve, the picture repeats along the whole number line.

This is a covering system. The divisor in each rule is its modulus. Our moduli are two, three, four, six, and twelve, each used once. Distinct means we cannot use the same modulus again with a different remainder.

Now impose a harder restriction. Every modulus must be at least six, and divide forty-five times some power of two. We may choose the power as large as we like, but the list must be finite. Can all integers still be covered?

The answer is no, for every power of two. The proof does not search through infinitely many powers. It checks a small initial stage exactly, then proves that a numerical obstruction survives every later doubling.

First separate the odd part from the powers of two. The odd divisors of forty-five are one, three, five, nine, fifteen, and forty-five. Every permitted modulus has one of these odd parts, multiplied by a power of two.

Represent a remainder modulo forty-five by two coordinates: its remainder modulo nine, and its remainder modulo five. There are nine columns and five rows. For example, seventeen sits in column eight and row two. Every integer residue has exactly one cell.

Each odd divisor now gives a shape of cells. A rule modulo nine fixes one column. A rule modulo five fixes one row. A rule modulo forty-five fixes a single cell. These are repeating arithmetic rules drawn as pieces on a board.

A rule modulo three selects three spaced columns, all with the same remainder modulo three. Modulo fifteen selects those three columns inside one row. Modulo one selects the whole board. These six types are all the pieces we need.

Next track parity. One board splits into two: an even branch and an odd branch. Modulo four, each splits again, giving four boards. Knowing the remainder modulo four and modulo forty-five identifies a remainder modulo one hundred and eighty.

A rule whose modulus is two to the power i times an odd divisor chooses a branch at depth i, and a piece type on that branch. Below that branch it keeps covering the same odd residues. Existing patterns are inherited by both children.

At each new depth, there is at most one new rule of each of the six types. Why? Reusing a type at the same depth would reuse the exact same modulus. Distinctness limits the new supply of pieces, even as the boards double.

Counting uncovered cells alone is not enough. Their arrangement matters. Instead, assign prices to pieces: fourteen for a whole board, seven for a three-column block, four for a row, two for a column, two for a short row, and one for a cell.

A board's cost is the cheapest total price of pieces covering its remaining cells. In this bookkeeping calculation, repeated piece types are allowed. That is a relaxed measuring tool; it does not allow repeated moduli in the actual covering problem.

Here is a real uncovered pattern from the retained check. It contains seventeen cells. Four columns cover them all, at price two each, for cost eight. The exact cost routine also checks that no cheaper combination of pieces can do it.

Suppose a new rule removes the highlighted column. Cover the remaining cells, then buy that column back. You have a cover of the original pattern. So removing a piece can lower the minimum cost by no more than the piece's own price.

Add the minimum costs of all current boards and call the total Q. Before any new rules, doubling the boards doubles Q exactly. The children inherit identical uncovered patterns, so each parent's cost appears twice.

Now spend the new rules. There is at most one piece of each type. Their prices add to thirty, which we call R. Together they can reduce the doubled cost by at most thirty. So the next Q is at least two Q minus R.

Here is the trap. If Q has already reached thirty, then the next value is at least two times thirty minus thirty: still thirty. Repeat the argument at every later depth. The cost can never fall to zero.

A completed covering has no uncovered cells, so every board costs zero. Therefore, once Q reaches R, no finite continuation can finish. That is the step turning a calculation at one small depth into a statement about arbitrarily large powers of two.

The remaining job is finite. At depth two there are four boards and thirteen allowed moduli, all dividing one hundred and eighty and at least six. Check every possible placement of those remainder rules, including choices that omit a modulus.

One price list is not enough for the retained proof. There are eleven lists. For every initial configuration, at least one list reaches its own threshold. The list that works can depend on the configuration. After choosing it, the same doubling inequality applies forever.

These four exact boards show why the eleventh list matters. Their uncovered cell counts are zero, seventeen, eighteen, and twenty-four. They survived the first ten tests. Now apply the prices we have been using to the same four patterns.

The empty board costs zero. The second costs eight, using four columns. The third costs twelve, using three rows. The fourth costs twelve, using six columns. The exact minima add to thirty-two, above the threshold of thirty.

Doubling this state therefore leaves cost at least thirty-four. Double again and it is at least thirty-eight. The obstruction persists. With another price list the same state can fall below its threshold, so multiple ways of measuring are doing real work.

The main C search visits four hundred and ninety-eight thousand, four hundred and sixty-four nodes, with zero survivors. A separate generic C implementation also finds zero. Independent Python covers one hundred and thirty-five roots and over four million nodes, again with zero survivors.

The proof combines those exact finite checks with the written doubling lemma. It is not a test of just a few large exponents. Controls check known coverings and the cost calculations, and deliberately incomplete result summaries are rejected. There is no Lean formalisation.

There is a surprising limit to the statement: an infinite distinct covering with these kinds of moduli exists. That does not contradict the theorem. At every finite stage, something remains uncovered, even though every particular integer can eventually be covered later.

Think carefully about the order of those statements. For each finite list, there is some missed integer. That is compatible with each integer appearing somewhere in an infinite list. There need not be one integer that escapes every stage.

Harrington, Klein, Lowrance and Trifonov posed this finite question and supplied the infinite construction. This result settles their Problem Two. It does not settle the separate minimum-eight problem or the exploratory case with odd part one hundred and thirty-five.

The conclusion uses every restriction. The list is finite. Moduli are distinct. Each is at least six. And all divide forty-five times a power of two. Under those conditions, every attempted covering leaves a gap, however far the power of two grows.

The central idea is a price that survives doubling. Exact enumeration proves every starting arrangement gets trapped by some price list. The inequality keeps it trapped forever. That is how a finite calculation can prove an infinite family of impossibility statements.

The source paper, eleven price vectors, recorded checks and editable animation accompany this video. Correctness confidence is high within the stated proof and computational model; the priority search is bounded. Narration uses a synthetic voice.
